cues.zh: 但我认为早就有充分的理由去质疑并重新评估这一切了。这种重新评估却从未真正发生过。但我会说，我认为我们现在已经到了一个节点，这在接下来的两到五年，甚至十年内真的会发生。我不觉得这部《楚门的世界》还能演多久了。

cues.en: where you lie about the real interest rates because the other two don't work anymore. And sort of a complicated way these things connect. cues.zh: 然后近几十年我们试图更精确地管理这些金融指标，尽管顺风根本不存在。让我把注意力放在两个对判断未来经济很重要的主题上。我很喜欢也许过度断言，但我要为物理学强力主张：物理学给了我们原子装置和核能。

cues.en: somehow we're in a new orchard and we're spending a lot of time exploring it, but we haven't found the low hanging fruit in biology. cues.zh: 不知怎么，我们在一片新果园里，花很多时间探索，但还没在生物学找到低垂的果实。而物理学果园则有点被我们穷尽了，因为发现的东西太奇异，比如两个黑洞相撞、第三代物质或夸克子结构，我们没法利用这些东西。我们是不是莫名处在两次革命之间？嗯，我想，我会说问题在于正在发生什么，而我

cues.zh: 我对那种理论有点怀疑。嗯，我也吃不准。比如如果你是研究弦理论的，甚至只是做应用实验物理的，我觉得你很难那么轻易就转向生物学。我是说，这些学科已经变得更加僵化了。从一个领域跨到另一个领域相当困难。我读本科时，还能看到一些

cues.en: you know, older professors who were polymaths who knew a lot about a lot of different things. This is, this is, I think the way one should really think of, you know, Watson and Crick or Feynman or, you know, or Teller, they, they, you know, they, they were certainly world-class in, in, in their field, but also like incredible in, in a lot of different fields. cues.zh: “你看，我们系根本没搞出什么名堂。这边这个系也没什么实质进展，那边那个系同样毫无突破。”这类人是非常非常危险的。我有个朋友90年代末在 Stanford 学物理。他的导师是 Stanford 的教授 Bob Laughlin，90年代末的一位天才物理学家，当时获得了诺贝尔物理学奖，但他陷入了

cues.zh: 那些毫无意义的虚假研究上。于是他开始去调查其他院系，首先就是斯坦福大学的生物系。你可以想象，这对 Laughlin 教授来说简直是一场灾难。他的研究生拿不到博士学位，他也拿不到经费了。哪怕拿过诺贝尔物理学奖也毫无用处，根本起不到任何保护作用。还有 Julian Schwinger，

cues.en: fell out of favor with the physics community despite being held in its highest regard and having a Nobel prize. And he used the epigram in a book where he wanted to redo quantum field theory around something he called source theory. He said, if you can't join them, beat them. And I think it comes as a shock to all of these people that there is no level you can rise to in the field that allows you to question the assumptions of that field. Right. It's, it's like, you know,
cues.zh: 尽管曾备受物理学界推崇，还拿过诺贝尔奖，但后来也失宠了。他在一本书里引用了一句警句，当时他想围绕一种被称为“源理论”的东西重构量子场论。他说：“如果你无法融入他们，那就击败他们。”我想对所有人来说，最震惊的莫过于：在这个领域里，无论你升到多高的地位，你都无权去质疑该领域的基本假设。对吧。就像，你懂的，

cues.en: you're sort of proving yourself, you're, you know, you're getting your PhD, you're getting your tenured position. And then at some point you think you would think that you've proven yourself and you can, you can talk about the whole and not just the parts, but you're never allowed to talk about more than the parts. You know, like the, um, the person in the university context, the, or the class of people who are supposed to talk about the whole, I would say our university presidents, because they are presiding over the whole of the university.
cues.zh: 你不断证明自己，拿到博士学位，拿到终身教职。然后到了某个阶段，你本以为自己已经证明了能力，可以去谈论整体而不仅仅是局部了，但你却永远只被允许谈论局部。而在大学的环境里，本该去纵观全局的人，或者说那类人，我认为应该是大学校长，因为他们主持着整所大学的全局。

cues.en: and they should be able to speak to what the nature of the whole is, what sort of progress the whole is making, what is the health of the progress of the whole. And we certainly do not pick university presidents who think critically about these questions at all. Well, I remember discussing with a president of a very highly regarded university,
cues.zh: 他们应该能够说明整体的本质是什么、整体取得了怎样的进展、整体的发展是否健康。但我们选拔大学校长时，显然根本不会选那些对这些问题有批判性思考的人。我记得曾经和一所顶尖大学的校长交流过，

cues.en: He came to me, he said, can you explain how your friend Peter Thiel thinks? Because I just had a conversation with him and I could not convince him that the universities were doing fantastically in this university in particular. Like, how does he come to this conclusion? And I said, well, look, Peter.
cues.zh: 他来找我，说：“你能解释一下你朋友 Peter Thiel 是怎么想的吗？因为我刚跟他聊过，我根本无法说服他大学运转得非常好，尤其是我们这所大学。他是怎么得出这种结论的？”我说：“好吧，Peter

cues.en: doesn't come, you know, with a PhD, but let me speak to you in your own language. I started going department by department talking about the problems of stagnation. It was very clear that there was no previous experience with any kind of informed person making such an argument. I mean, this was a zero day exploit. But it's all, yeah, but it's, but you know, in some sense, if you're a president of a university, you know, you
cues.zh: 虽然没有博士学位，但让我用你们学术界的行话来跟你聊聊。”我开始逐个院系剖析停滞不前的问题。很明显，他之前从未遇到过任何懂行的人提出过这种论点。这简直就像一次零日漏洞攻击。但话说回来，某种程度上，作为一名大学校长，

cues.en: you should probably don't want to talk to people that dangerous. You want to avoid them and you don't want to have such disruptive thoughts because you have to convince the government or alumni or whoever to keep donating money that everything's wonderful and great. And I think one has to go back quite a long time to even identify any university presidents in the United States who said things that were distinctive or interesting or powerful.
cues.zh: 你大概并不想和这么危险的人交谈。你会想避开他们，也不想产生这种颠覆性的想法，因为你得向政府、校友或所有人证明一切都很美好、很棒，好让他们继续捐款。我觉得要追溯到很久以前，才能在全美找到哪怕一位能讲出独到、深刻或有力见解的大学校长了。

cues.en: You know, there was, you know, there was Larry Summers at Harvard, you know, a decade and a half ago and tried to do like the most minuscule critiques imaginable and got, you know, crucified. But, uh, you know, I don't think of, you know, I don't think of Summers as a particularly revolutionary thinker. Well, he, he was possessed of an idea that the intellectual elite in which he undoubtedly saw himself a part of had the right
cues.zh: 你看，十五年前哈佛的 Larry Summers，不过是提了点微不足道的批评，结果就被千夫所指。但我并不觉得 Summers 是个多么激进的思想家。其实他只是抱有一种想法，认为自己身处其中的知识精英有权

cues.en: to transgress boundaries. And I think what's stunning about this is the extent to which this breed of outspoken, disruptive intellectual has no place left inside of the system from which to speak. But it's not that surprising. Like in a healthy system, you can have wild descent and it's not threatening because everyone knows the system is healthy. In an unhealthy system,
cues.zh: 去打破界限。我觉得令人震惊的是，体制内居然已经没有容纳这种直言不讳、颠覆性知识分子发声的立足之地了。但这也并不意外。比如在健康的体制中，即便有激烈的异议也不会构成威胁，因为大家知道体制是健康的。但在不健康的体制中，

cues.en: the dissent becomes much more dangerous. And I think it's not that surprising. One riff I have on this is always, if you think of a left-wing person as someone who's critical of the structures of our society, there's a sense in which we have almost no left-wing professors left. That's right. The Noam Chomsky is still there as
cues.zh: 异议就会变得极其危险。我觉得这一点也不奇怪。对此我常有的一个想法是，如果你把左翼人士定义为批判我们社会结构的人，那么在某种程度上，我们几乎已经没有真正的左翼教授了。没错。Noam Chomsky 依然还在，

cues.en: sort of a last remnant of some clade that no longer exists. Left wing in the sense of, let's say just being critical of the institutions they're part of. Right. And there may be some that are much older. So if you're maybe in your eighties, we can, you know, we can pretend to ignore you or, you know, it's just what happens to people in their eighties. Sure. But, but I don't, I don't see, you know, younger professors in their, let's say forties who are deeply critical of the, of the university structure. I think it's just, it's just not
cues.zh: 就像是某个已经消亡的派系留下的最后遗迹。这里的左翼，指的是敢于批评自己所属体制的人。对。也许还有一些年纪更大的。如果你八十多岁了，大家可能就当没听见，觉得八十岁老人就是这样。确实。但我没看到年轻一代，比如四十几岁的教授，会深刻批评大学的体制结构。我觉得这根本就——

cues.en: you can't have that. It's like, again, if you come back to something as reductionist as the ever escalating student debt, the bigger the debt gets, you can sort of think, what is the 1.6 trillion? What does it pay for? And in a sense it pays for $1.6 trillion worth of lies about how great the system is. And so the more the debt goes, the crazier the system gets, but also the more you have to tell the lies and these things sort of go together.
cues.zh: 你不可能容忍这种事。就比如，如果回到不断攀升的学生贷款这个直观问题上，债务规模越大，你就会琢磨：这 1.6 万亿美元究竟买了什么？某种意义上，它买了价值 1.6 万亿美元的谎言，用来吹嘘这套体制有多好。债务越多，体制就越疯狂，而你也就越得撒谎，这两者是绑在一起的。

cues.en: It's not a stable sequence. At some point, this breaks. Again, I would bet on, you know, a decade, not a century. Well, this is the fascinating thing. You, of course, famously started the Teal Fellowship as a program, which correct me if I'm wrong on this. 2005 is when student debt became non-dischargeable, even in bankruptcy. The Bush 43 bankruptcy revision. Right. Now that is- Yes. And so if you don't pay off your student loans,
cues.zh: 这种状态是不稳定的。到了某个时间点，它一定会崩溃。我打赌这只需要十年，而不是一个世纪。这正是耐人寻味的地方。你发起 Thiel Fellowship 项目也是众所周知，如果我记错了请纠正我。2005 年，学生贷款变成了就算破产也无法免除的债务。小布什总统时期的破产法修订案。没错。那简直是——是的。所以如果你不还清学生贷款，

cues.en: when you're 65, the government will garnish your social security wages to pay off your student debt. Right, this is amazing that this exists in a modern society. And of course, well, so let me ask, am I right that you were attacking what was necessary to keep the college mythology going and you were frightened that college might be innovating some of our sort of most dynamic minds?
cues.zh: 到了 65 岁，政府甚至会扣留你的社会保障金来抵偿学贷。天哪，这种事居然会存在于现代社会。当然，那么我想问，你当时攻击的是维持大学神话所必需的东西，而且你担心大学可能会压制我们最活跃的一些头脑，我这样理解对吗？

cues.en: Well, I think there's sort of a lot of different critiques one can have of the universities. I think the debt one is a very simple, very simple one. It's always dangerous to be burdened with too much debt. It sort of does limit your freedom of action. And it seems especially pernicious to do this super early in your career. And so if out of the gate, you owe a hundred thousand dollars and
cues.zh: 我觉得大家对大学可以有很多不同的批评。其中学生贷款这个批评就非常简单明了。背负过多债务总是很危险的，它确实会在某种程度上限制你的行动自由。而在职业生涯刚起步时就这样，似乎尤其有害。所以如果你一踏入社会就欠了十万美元，

cues.en: it's never clear you can get out of that hole. That's going to either demotivate you or it's going to push you into maybe slightly higher paying, very uncreative professions of the sort that are probably less good at moving our whole society forwards. And so I think, yeah, so I think the whole thing is extraordinarily pernicious. And it is...
cues.zh: 而且根本看不到还清的希望。这要么会让你丧失动力，要么会逼着你去从事那些可能薪水稍高、但毫无创造力的职业，而这类工作往往不太能推动整个社会的进步。所以我觉得，是的，整件事危害极大。而且……

cues.en: It was one of these things where, and I started talking about this back in 2010, it was already like, it was controversial, but it was not like, younger people all agreed with me. The younger people did. And it's a decade later, it's a lot crazier. We haven't yet completely won, but.
cues.zh: 这事儿就是这样，我早在2010年就开始聊这个话题了，当时就挺有争议，但也并非所有年轻人都赞同我。不过确实有年轻人认同。十年过去了，情况变得疯狂得多。虽然我们还没彻底扭转局面，但是……

cues.en: But I think there are sort of more and more people who agree with us. I think at this point, the Gen X parents of college students tend to agree. Whereas I would say the baby boomer parents, you know, 15 years ago would not have agreed. The 2008 crisis was a big watershed in this too, where you could say the tracking debt, you know, roughly made sense as long as everything, all the tracked careers worked. And 2008 really blew up, you know, consulting, banking.
cues.zh: 但我觉得赞同我们的人越来越多了。我认为目前大学生的X世代父母往往会认同这一点。而换作15年前的婴儿潮一代父母，他们是不会同意的。2008年的危机在这方面也是一个巨大的分水岭，你可以说只要按部就班的传统职业道路走得通，背负这种定向债务大体上就还说得过去。但2008年彻底摧毁了咨询和银行业等。

cues.en: So a number of the more track professions got blown up. And so that was kind of a watershed. Now, something that just, I mean, this is incredibly dangerous, but also therefore quite interesting. If you imagine that the baby boomers have in some sense, in order to keep the structure of the university going, have loaded it up with administrators, have hiked the tuition much faster than even medical inflation, let alone general inflation, this becomes a crushing debt
cues.zh: 很多原本按部就班的传统职业都被打乱了。所以那算是一个分水岭。现在有件事，我是说这极其危险，但也正因如此而非常耐人寻味。设想一下，婴儿潮一代在某种程度上为了维持大学的运转架构，塞满了行政管理人员，学费的涨幅甚至远超医疗通胀，更不用说普通通胀了，这就变成了沉重的债务负担，

cues.en: problem for people who are entering the system. I saw a recent article that said that the, um, company that, uh, I think it's called seeking arrangements, which introduces, um, older men and women with money to younger men and women with a need for money for some sort of ambiguous hybridized dating companionship financial transfer. And
cues.zh: 压在了每一个进入这个体系的人身上。我最近看到一篇文章，说有一家公司，好像叫 SeekingArrangement，专门撮合有钱的年长男女与缺钱的年轻男女，建立某种兼具约会、陪伴与金钱资助的暧昧关系。并且……

cues.en: The claim was that lots of students were using this supposed sugar daddying and sugar mommy, I don't know what the terminology is, in order to alleviate their debt burden. It's almost as if the baby boomers in so creating a system are subjecting their own children to things that are pushing them towards a gray area a few clicks before you get to honest prostitution.
cues.zh: 报道称，许多学生正是利用这种所谓的“糖爹”和“糖妈”关系（我不太清楚确切叫法），来减轻他们的债务负担。这就好像婴儿潮一代一手打造了这样的制度，将自己的下一代推向了灰色地带，离真正的卖淫只差最后几步。

cues.en: I don't want to impute too much intentionality. I don't know how this happened. I think a lot of these, it was mostly emergent, mostly these things people, yeah, that we had sort of somewhat cancerous, we don't distinguish real growth from cancerous growth. And then once the cancer sort of metastasizes at a certain size, you sort of somehow try to keep the whole thing going and it doesn't make that much sense.
cues.zh: 我不想把这过多归咎于某种蓄意。我不知道这是怎么发生的。我觉得其中很多主要是自然演变出来的，多半是大家……对，我们有点像患了癌，分不清真正的增长和癌性病变。一旦癌细胞扩散到一定程度，你就会想方设法去维持整个系统的运转，但这其实没什么意义了。

cues.en: But yes, look, I think one of the reasons, one of the challenges on our side, let's be a little bit more self-critical here on this is that the question we always are confronted with, well, what is the alternative? How do you actually do something? And it's not obvious what the individual alternatives are. On an individual level, if you get into an elite university,
cues.zh: 不过确实，你看，我觉得我们这边的挑战之一——我们在这点上稍微做些自我反省吧——那就是我们总会面临这个问题：“那有什么替代方案？到底该怎么做？”对个人来说，替代路线并不明朗。在个人层面上，如果你考进了一所顶尖名校，

cues.en: it probably still makes sense to go. It probably doesn't make sense to go to number 100 or something like this. But so there is sort of a way it can still work individually, even if it does not work for our country as a whole. And so there are sort of all these challenges in coming up with alternate tracks. I think in software, there's some degree to which people are gonna be hired if they're just good at coding.
cues.zh: 去读大概率还是划算的。但如果去读排名第100名左右的学校，可能就不太划算了。所以对于个人来说，它在某种程度上仍说得通，哪怕对我们整个国家来说并不是这样。因此，在开拓替代路线上面临着各种挑战。我觉得在软件行业，只要你代码写得好，多多少少是会被录用的。

cues.en: And it's not quite as critical that they have a computer science degree. Can we do this in other careers, other fields? I would tend to think one could. It's been slow to happen. Well, so you and I have been excited about a great number of things that have been taking place outside of the institutional system. But one of the things that I continue to be mystified by is that we are somewhat politically divided, where you are well known as a conservative. And I really come from
cues.zh: 有没有计算机学位倒没那么关键。那在其他职业、其他领域能这么做吗？我倾向于认为是可以的，只是推进得一直很慢。话说回来，你我都对体制系统之外正在发生的很多事情感到兴奋。但有件事一直让我很困惑：我们在政治立场上其实有些分歧，众所周知你是保守派，而我其实骨子里

cues.en: a fairly radical progressive streak. So we have this common view of a lot of the problems, but sometimes we come to very different ideas about how those problems should be solved. Do you want to maybe just try riffing, figuring out, like assume that we somehow found ourselves in a position of some degree of power with an ability to direct a little bit more than we have currently. What would you do to create the preconditions
cues.zh: 是个相当激进的进步派。我们对许多问题有着相同的看法，但有时关于如何解决这些问题，想法却大相径庭。你愿不愿意试着展开聊聊、琢磨一下：假设我们不知怎么地掌握了一定的权力，能比现在有更多的指导权。你会做些什么来创造那些前提条件——

cues.en: So not necessarily picking particular projects, but what would you try to do to create the preconditions where people are really dreaming about futures, both at a technological level, family formation, making our civil society healthier? Where would you start to work first? Well, there are a lot of things that...
cues.zh: 不一定是去挑具体的项目，而是你会如何去创造前提条件，让人们真正去憧憬未来，无论是在技术层面、组建家庭，还是让我们的公民社会更健康？你会先从哪里着手？嗯，有很多事情……

cues.en: So I'm always a little bit uncomfortable with this sort of question because. You can train on me too. Because, you know, I feel like, you know, we're not going to be dictators of the United States. And then, you know, there are all sorts of things we could do for dictators. But certainly, look, I would look at the college debt thing very seriously. I would say that, you know, it's just chargeable in bankruptcy.
cues.zh: 我对这类问题总是有点不太自在，因为……你也可以拿我开刀。因为我觉得，我们不可能成为美国的独裁者。要是独裁者的话，能做的事可就多了。不过说实在的，我会非常严肃地对待大学助学贷款这个问题。我会认为，它理应可以在破产中被清偿。

cues.en: if people go bankrupt, then part of the debt has to be paid for by the university that did it. There has to be some sort of local accountability. So this would be sort of a more right-wing answer. The left-wing answers, we should socialize the debt in some ways, and the universities should never pay for it, which would be more the Sanders-Warren approach. So that would be one version. I think there is...
cues.zh: 如果有人破产了，那引发这笔债务的大学就得承担一部分。必须得有某种地方层面的问责机制。这算是偏右翼的做法。左翼的做法则是，我们应该以某种方式将债务社会化，而大学永远不必为此买单，这更偏向 Sanders 和 Warren 的主张。所以这是一种方案。我认为……

cues.en: I think there is, I think one of the main ways inequality has manifested in our society in the last 20, 30 years. I think it's more stagnation than inequality. But just on the inequality side, it's the runaway housing costs. And there's a baby boomer version where you have super strict zoning laws so that the house prices go up and the house is your nest egg. It's not a place to live. It's your nest egg for retirement. And I would try to figure out some ways to dial.
cues.zh: 我认为，在过去二三十年里，不平等在社会中的主要表现形式之一……其实我觉得停滞更甚于不平等。但单就指不平等而言，就是失控的住房成本。婴儿潮一代的做法是推行极其严格的区划法，以此推高房价，让房子成了养老钱。它不再只是个住处，而是你的养老老本。而我会试着想办法……

cues.en: dial that stuff back massively. And that's probably intergenerational transfer where it's bad for the asset prices of baby boomer homeowners, but better for younger people to get started in sort of family formation or starting households. What do you think about the idea of a CED, a college equivalency degree, where you can prove that you have
cues.zh: 想办法去大幅逆转这种局面。这大概是一种代际财富转移，它会损害婴儿潮一代房主的资产价格，但对年轻人组建家庭或置业成家更有利。你觉得“大学同等学力证书”（CED）这个构想怎么样？通过它你可以证明自己拥有……

cues.en: a level of knowledge that would be equivalent, let's say, to a graduating Harvard chemistry major, right, or a fraction thereof, where you have the ability to prove that through some sort of online delivery mechanism, you can- Great idea. I love it. Yeah. I think it's very hard to implement. Again, I think these things are hard to do. Well, again- Great idea. There's a possibility of- But look, we have all these people who have something like Stockholm Syndrome, where they, you know, if you-
cues.zh: 具备与哈佛化学专业毕业生相当的知识水平，哪怕是一部分也行。只要你能通过某种在线考核机制来证明这一点，你就能——极好的想法，我很赞同。是的，但我认为落地极难。话说回来，这些事做起来都很棘手。没错，不过——这是个绝妙的想法，存在这种可能——但你看，很多人都患有某种“斯德哥尔摩综合征”，如果你……

cues.en: if you've got a Harvard chemistry degree, right? And if you suspect that, you know, actually the knowledge could be had by a lot of people. And if it's just a set of tests, you have to pass that your degree would be a lot less special. You will, you will resist this very, very hard. You know, if you're, if you're in an, in an HR department or in a company hiring people, you will want to hire people who went

cues.zh: 被杀戮的事实，恰恰是因为那数百万人的被杀戮。只要你愿意杀死数百万人，那就是一个信号，表明你正在建设乌托邦，正在构建一个伟大的新社会。而一旦停下来，就会变成 Brezhnev 时代那种死气沉沉的状态。那根本无法振奋人心。后来人们从崇拜 Stalin 转向了 Mao 或 Castro，但那种暴力本身具有一种非凡的吸引力，我认为极具吸引力。

cues.en: But then also, if you think about it, it's very undesirable. I think that they're, it's so fascinating that we actually finally get to something like this. I think that that is a correct description of part of the communist movement, but not all of the communist movement. There were a lot of people I think in the, just my own family was certainly involved in far left politics and some of it probably dipped into communism. What my sense of it was is that,
cues.zh: 但仔细想想，这又是极度不可取的。我们终于探讨到这类问题，真的很有意思。我认为这准确描述了共产主义运动的一部分，但并不是全部。当时有很多人，比如我自己的家族，肯定参与过极左政治，其中一部分可能还涉足过共产主义。我的感觉是，

cues.en: there was a period in the 30s where people realized that there had to be coordinated social action and that there were people who were too vulnerable. And that that somehow got wrapped up in all of the things that Stalin was talking about that sounded positive if you didn't know the reality. So for example, Paul Robeson, you know, a hero of the left, you know, was extolling Stalin's virtues openly.
cues.zh: 在 30 年代有那么一段时期，人们意识到必须有协同的社会行动，也意识到有些人太过弱势。如果你不了解背后的现实，这种理念不知怎的就和 Stalin 口中那些听起来很美好的说辞捆绑在了一起。比如左翼英雄 Paul Robeson，就曾公开颂扬 Stalin 的美德。

cues.en: My guess is, is that he didn't fully understand what had happened, that he had gotten involved in an earlier era and that as things became known and progressed, there was a point at which many people suddenly opened their eyes and said, I've been making excuses for the Soviet Union because at least it had the hope. I mean, you know, there were American blacks, for example, who moved to Moscow because of the hope that it was going to be a racially more equal society.
cues.zh: 我猜他并没有完全明白到底发生了什么，他在早期就卷入其中，而随着真相大白和事态发展，很多人突然醒悟过来并说道：我之前一直在为苏联找借口，至少是因为它曾寄托着希望。要知道，比如当时有些美国黑人移居莫斯科，就是怀着那里会是一个种族更平等的社会的希望。

cues.en: My own family, I would say, was talking about interracial marriage and open support of homosexuality, female access to birth control. Those things were associated with the Communist Party, and a lot of those ideas are now commonplace, but we forget that once upon a time, only the Communists were willing to dance with these things. Yes, I don't want to make this too ad hominem, but I want to say that people
cues.zh: 就拿我自己的家庭来说，他们当年就在谈论跨种族通婚、公开支持同性恋，以及女性获取避孕手段的权利。这些在当时都是和共产党联系在一起的，如今很多这种观念已司空见惯，但我们忘了，曾经只有共产党人愿意接纳这些主张。是的，我不想把这变成人身攻击，但我想说，

cues.en: like your family were likely very intelligent people, but were somehow still always the useful idiots. And there was no country where the communists actually came to power, where people like those in your family actually got to make the decisions. And somehow, like maybe there were indirect ways.
cues.zh: 像你家人这样的人很可能非常聪明，但在某种程度上却始终是“有用的白痴”。而且在所有共产党真正掌权的国家里，像你家人这样的人从未真正拥有过决策权。也许在某些间接层面上，

cues.en: that it was helpful or beneficial in countries that did not become communist, but in countries that actually became communist, it didn't actually ever seem to work out for those people. I definitely think that there was some sense that they were fooled and duped in this situation, but by the same token, not wanting to make this too ad hominem.
cues.zh: 这对那些没有走向共产主义的国家有所助益，但在真正建立起共产政权的国家里，那些人的下场似乎从来都不太好。我确实认为，在某种程度上他们是被愚弄和利用了，但同样，我也不想把这搞成人身攻击。

cues.en: You know, as a gay man, I think that a lot of your rights would have been seen much earlier by the communists who were earlier to that party. I think that, um, to an extent, uh, some of the things that we just take for granted as part of living in a tolerant society were really not found outside. And so if you were trying to dine a la carte, um, maybe you could take something from the commie buffet. You could take something from the anti-communist buffet.
cues.zh: 要知道，作为一名同性恋者，我认为你的很多权益原本会被更早涉足这一领域的共产党人所认可。我认为，在某种程度上，那些我们如今在包容性社会中习以为常的事情，在外界其实根本找不到。所以如果你想按需选择，也许你可以从共产党那头各取所需一点，也可以从反共阵营那头取一点。

cues.en: And you could steal a little from regular party politics. Of course, the Dixiecrats were not exactly the most racially progressive group in the world. Things were very different and there was no clear place to turn. Yeah, it's always easy for us to judge people in the past too harshly. So I think that's a good generalization. I would say that there's something about
cues.zh: 你还可以从常规的党派政治中借鉴一点。当然，迪克西民主党人可绝算不上世界上在种族问题上最进步的群体。当时情况大不相同，没有一个明确的方向可供求助。是的，我们总是很容易对过去的人苛加指责。所以我觉得这个概括很到位。我想说的是，关于革命，

cues.en: the revolution, the extreme revolutionary movements that always seem to be, from my point of view, the violence was always too much. And it's a package deal, but I don't like the violence part of the package. And that's the part that at the end of the day makes me think the package would not have been worth it. So what I would like to do is to take a quick break and I would like to come back on exactly this point because it's the point where I feel that perhaps you are
cues.zh: 那些极端的革命运动在我看来，其暴力程度总是太过火了。而这往往是个全盘打包的方案，可我并不喜欢其中的暴力部分。正是这一部分，最终让我觉得这个全盘方案根本不值。所以我想先插播一段短暂的休息，稍后我想就这一点继续深入，因为我觉得在关于

cues.en: least understood by the outside world in terms of what we've been talking about, both growth and progress on the one hand and violence on the other. So when we come back, we'll pick it up with Peter Thiel. Thank you. Thanks. Welcome back to The Portal. I'm here with my friend and employer, Peter Thiel, for this, our inaugural interview episode. And we've just gotten to a point which I think...
cues.zh: 一方面是增长与进步，另一方面是暴力这一话题上，外界对你的误解可能是最深的。广告之后，我们将继续与 Peter Thiel 畅谈。谢谢。谢谢。欢迎回到 The Portal。我是主持人，今天在我们首期访谈节目中，和我坐在一起的是我的朋友兼雇主 Peter Thiel。我们刚刚聊到了一个我认为……

cues.en: I hope people who've been tracking your career, your books, your thought process are gonna find interesting because I think it's the thing that if I had to guess would be the thing that people least understand about you or maybe they have wrong the most. Ever since I've known you, your focus has weirdly been reduction of violence across a great number of different topics at a level that I don't think has leaked out into the public's understanding
cues.zh: 我希望一直关注你的事业、著作和思考过程的人会觉得有意思，因为如果我猜得没错，这可能是人们最不理解你、或误解最深的一点。从我认识你以来，你的关注点一直奇怪地落在许多不同议题上的减少暴力，而且这个层次我觉得还没有渗入公众的理解

cues.en: of you and what causes you to make the choices you make. How do you see growth as attached to reduction of violence? Well, I think that it's very hard to see how anything like the kinds of societies we have in Western Europe, the United States, could function without growth. I think the way...
cues.zh: 也就是对你、以及是什么让你做出这些选择的理解。你如何看待增长与减少暴力之间的联系？嗯，我觉得很难想象，像西欧和美国这样的社会，如果没有增长该如何运转。我觉得方式……

cues.en: sort of a parliamentary Republican democracy works as you have a group of people sitting around the table. They craft complicated legislation and there's a lot of horse trading. And as long as the pie is growing, you can give something to everybody. When the pie stops growing, it becomes a zero sum dynamic and the legislative process does not work. And so the sort of democratic types of parliamentary systems we've had for the last 200
cues.zh: 议会制共和民主大致是这样运作的：一群人围坐在桌边，制定复杂的立法，进行大量政治交易。只要蛋糕在变大，你就能给每个人分点东西。蛋糕一旦停止变大，就变成零和动态，立法过程就行不通了。所以我们过去 200

cues.en: 250 years have mapped onto this period of rapid growth. We had sort of a very bad experiment in the 1930s where the growth stopped, at least sort of in the economic sense. And the system, you know, systems became fascist or communist. It didn't, it doesn't actually work. And so I, I suspect that if we're in for a period of long growth, I don't think
cues.zh: 250 年来，一直对应着这个快速增长时期。我们在 1930 年代做过一个很糟的实验，增长停止了，至少在经济意义上如此。然后制度，你知道，制度变成了法西斯或共产主义。它没有、它实际上行不通。所以我怀疑，如果我们进入一个长期增长停滞的时期，我不认为

cues.en: I don't think our our kind of government can work. I think there is a prospect of all sorts of forms of violence, more violence by the state against its citizens. There may be more zero sum wars globally or there may be other ways things are super deformed to pacify people. So maybe maybe everyone just smokes marijuana all day. But that's that's also kind of deformed. But I think I think a world without growth is either going to be a much more violent or a much more deformed world. And
cues.zh: 我不认为我们这种政府能运转。我认为可能会出现各种形式的暴力，国家对其公民施加更多暴力。全球可能出现更多零和战争，或者用其他方式把事情极度扭曲来安抚民众。所以也许，也许大家就整天抽大麻。但那也是一种扭曲。但我认为，没有增长的世界要么会暴力得多，要么会扭曲得多。而且

cues.en: And again, it's, uh, you know, it's not the case that growth simply solves all problems. So you can have very rapid growth and it can still, you can still have the problem of violence. You can still, you can still have, uh, bad things that can happen, but that's our only chance without growth. Um, I think, uh, I think it's very hard to see how you have a good future. Now, in some sense, whenever I hear you interpreted in the prime, I mean, look, you are, you have to know that there's a version of, of you.
cues.zh: 而且，呃，你知道，增长并不是简单解决所有问题。所以你可以有非常快的增长，但仍然、你仍然会有暴力问题。你仍然、仍然会有，呃，坏事发生，但那是我们唯一的机会；没有增长，嗯，我觉得，呃，我觉得很难看到你怎么会有一个好的未来。现在，某种意义上，每当我听到别人在黄金时段节目里解读你，我的意思是，你看，你必须知道，存在一个版本的你。

cues.en: that exists in the minds of pundits and the commentariat that just loves to paint you as if you were a cartoon villain. And I always think that for those people who are actually confused about you, as opposed to those who wish to be confused about you, it's as if you're looking through a window and they're looking at the reflection in the window, not understanding what it is that you're focused on.
cues.zh: 这存在于专家和评论圈的脑海中，他们就喜欢把你描绘成卡通片里的反派。我总觉得，对于那些真正对你感到困惑的人，而不是那些故意装糊涂的人来说，这就好像你在透过窗户看外面，而他们却只盯着窗户上的倒影，根本不明白你真正关注的是什么。

cues.en: Why do you think it is that almost nobody sees your preoccupation with violence reduction? Well, I think it's hard for me to come with a good answer to these sort of sociological questions. I think people generally don't think of the problem of violence as quite as central as I think it is. I think it's a very deep
cues.zh: 你觉得为什么几乎没有人看到你对减少暴力的专注？嗯，我觉得对于这类社会学问题，我很难给出一个确切的答案。我认为大众通常并不觉得暴力问题像我认为的那样处于核心地位。我觉得在人类层面上，

cues.en: problem on a human level. If you think of sort of this mimetic element to human nature where we copy one another, we want the things other people want. And there's a lot of room for conflict. And if it's not channeled very carefully, a violent conflict in human relationships and in human societies, between human societies. And this is sort of, I think, a very
cues.zh: 这是一个非常深刻的问题。如果你想想人性的这种模仿机制，我们互相模仿，渴望别人想要的东西。这就留下了巨大的冲突空间。如果不加以极其审慎的引导，就会演变成人际关系、人类社会内部以及社会之间的暴力冲突。我认为这算是一个非常、

cues.en: very deep problem. And it's not sort of Christian anthropology, but you also have the same in Machiavelli. There are sort of a lot of different traditions where human beings are, if not evil, they're at least dangerous. And I think the sort of softer anthropological biases that a lot of people have in sort of late modernity or in the enlightenment world are
cues.zh: 非常深刻的问题。这不仅存在于基督教人类学中，在马基雅维利那里也有同样的观点。在很多不同的传统中，人类即便不算邪恶，至少也是危险的。而我认为在后现代或启蒙运动的世界里，很多人抱有的那种偏软性的人类学偏见是，

cues.en: that humans are by nature good, they're by nature peaceful. And that's not the norm. So that might be sort of a general bias people have is that people can't be this violent. It's not this deep a problem. It's a problem other people have. There's some bad people who are violent, but it's not a general problem. You know, one of the things that I think has been fascinating to me in, you know,
cues.zh: 人天性本善，天性爱好和平。但事实并非如此。所以大家普遍存在的一种偏见可能就是：人不可能这么暴力。这没那么严重，是别人的问题，只是少数坏人才崇尚暴力，这不是普遍问题。你知道，我觉得有一点让我很着迷，就是，

cues.en: I mean, effectively, I didn't know you when I was young, and this feels like a lifelong friendship that got started way late in my life. And one of the things that kind of was surprising to me is that my coming from a Jewish background, you're coming from a German background. I think both of us were sensitized by the horrors of World War II, which, I mean, obviously the problem for the Jews is very clear, but...
cues.zh: 其实我年轻时并不认识你，但这段友谊给我的感觉，就像是一段在人生后半程才开始的终生挚友之交。让我有点惊讶的一件事是，我是犹太背景，而你是德国背景。我想我们俩都对二战的恐怖极为敏感，对于犹太人来说，问题显而易见，但是……

cues.en: the fact that Germany never really recovered its proud intellectual traditions that had gotten bound up in a level of mechanized and planned violence, you know, is a decimation of a great intellectual tradition. And one of the things we've talked about in the past is whether the twilight of living memory of the Holocaust should be used for some more profound German-Jewish reconciliation, that these are two communities that have held
cues.zh: 德国在深陷那种高度机械化、有预谋的暴力之后，其实再也没能真正恢复其引以为傲的知识分子传统，这摧毁了一个伟大的思想传统。我们过去讨论过的一点是，在犹太大屠杀亲历者记忆消逝的暮年，是否应该推动一场更深刻的德犹和解，因为从模仿竞争的角度来看，这两个群体有着

cues.en: somewhat similar thought processes from the perspective of mimetic competition, maybe there was a problem that they were doomed to run into each other, but that in some sense, there are two wounds that need to be healed now that all of the original participants are either quite elderly or gone. Do you think that that is informing our conversation? Well, I think there's certainly...
cues.zh: 某种相似的思维方式，也许注定会产生碰撞。但从某种意义上说，既然所有当事人要么垂垂老矣，要么已经离世，现在这两处伤口都需要愈合。你觉得这是否在潜移默化地影响着我们的对话？嗯，我认为肯定有……

cues.en: an element of that between the two of us. I think that there's probably a degree to which the history was so traumatic that people still understate this aspect. There was something about late 19th century, early 20th century Germany where the...
cues.zh: 我们两人之间也有这种感觉。我觉得历史可能太令人痛苦了，以至于人们至今仍在低估这一方面。19世纪末、20世纪初的德国有一种特质，当时……

cues.en: Judaism was better integrated into the society than in many other places. And there was something very synergistic, very, very generative about that. And and and then, you know, getting at all these ways that the that it was lost are very, very hard to do. You know, it's it's sort of a a sort of social democratic response to
cues.zh: 犹太人比在很多其他地方都更好地融入了社会。那种融合非常协同、极具创造力。而要去探讨失去这一切的种种方式，真的非常困难。你知道，面对希特勒时代和大屠杀，

cues.en: the Hitler era and the Holocaust was sort of radically egalitarian. Everybody's equal. You shouldn't kill people. Everybody's equally valuable. And yet in some ways, Hitler killed the best people. And so there's a way in which the social democratic response to what happened doesn't even come up to the terrible thing that happened. So in an egalitarian society, well, we don't have as quite as many people. We're all equal. Nothing's really changed.
cues.zh: 社会民主主义的回应在某种程度上是激进平等的。人人平等，不能杀人，人人都有同样的价值。但在某些方面，希特勒杀掉的是最优秀的一批人。所以社会民主主义对那场灾难的回应，甚至都没能正视其可怕之处。在一个平等的社会里，就算人数变少了，但大家都是平等的，好像并没有真正改变什么。

cues.en: But well, maybe you have no Jewish people left in Germany and there's a lot less dynamism in the society as a result. And that's something that people still can't say in Germany because that's that's right. You feel like it's, uh, you know, like if I say it, people won't, you know, they won't, they won't contradict it or anything. But, um, but it's, uh, it's, uh, you know, it's, it's, it's sort of profoundly, profoundly uncomfortable. So I think, I think there is a sense, uh,
cues.zh: 但实际上，德国可能几乎没有犹太人了，社会的活力因此大不如前。而这也是如今在德国人们依然无法公开言说的，确实如此。你会觉得，如果我提出来，人们不会反驳，但是……这会让人感到极度的不适。所以我认为确实存在一种感觉，

cues.en: Yeah, that, you know, it's, there's sort of all these strange ways that Germany is still under the shadow of Hitler. Even, you know, the ways that people are trying to, you know, exercise Hitler, you know, in some ways have deformed the society where you can't, you can't go back to the things that, you know, worked incredibly well in pre-World War I Germany. There was probably a lot, there was unhealthy and wrong with it too, but yeah, there's a sense that something,
cues.zh: 那就是德国在各种奇怪的层面上，依然笼罩在希特勒的阴影之下。甚至人们试图驱除希特勒影响的那些方式，在某种程度上反而扭曲了社会，让你再也回不到一战前德国那种运转极佳的状态。虽然当时可能也有很多病态和错误的地方，但确实让人觉得，

cues.en: something very big has been lost. And there probably are a Jewish version of this that one could articulate as well. But yeah, I think there's something about the synergy that's very powerful and that's quite missing. So from my side of the fence, I was just listening on NPR to a description of Fiddler on the Roof being put on by Joel Gray in Yiddish. And the sound of, you know,
cues.zh: 失去了某些极其重要的东西。或许从犹太人的角度也能表达出类似的情感。但我认为那种协同效应非常强大，而现在它彻底缺失了。就我个人而言，我刚在 NPR 上听到一段介绍，讲的是 Joel Gray 用意第绪语排演《屋顶上的提琴手》。听到那种……

cues.en: Jewish middle-high German. There's something about it that is shocking in today's era. And so there's been a Jewish loss. I felt this a couple of times. I avoided, to be honest, going to Germany because I didn't want to run into old people and wonder where they had been. But eventually, at Soros invitation, found myself at a conference in Berlin. And when I checked into the hotel,
cues.zh: 犹太式的中古高地德语。在当今时代听到那种声音，有一种令人震撼的感觉。这也是犹太文化的一种丧失。我有过几次这种体会。说实话，我以前一直避免去德国，因为我不想碰上老年人，然后忍不住去琢磨他们当年做过什么。但后来应 Soros 的邀请，我还是去柏林参加了一场会议。在酒店办理入住时，

cues.en: I heard my last name pronounced in impeccable German. And it was both a horrible feeling and a wonderful feeling. Like somehow, weirdly, something was home. Or I went to a restaurant near Checkpoint Charlie with my wife, and I was missing a fork. And the person spoke no English. And I remembered from some old story of my father. And I asked for a Gupel, which I guess is the Yiddish for fork.

cues.en: I was convinced that Trump was going to be such a wake up call that the democratic party was going to, you know, go behind a closed door and say, we cannot let this happen again. We have to look honestly at how we got beat, what this represents, what it means, and what we're going to do next time. And the idea that we were going to double or triple down on some of the stuff that didn't work never even occurred to me. I had no idea that that party was so far gone that
cues.zh: 我曾确信，Trump 会是一场如此强烈的警钟，以至于民主党会关起门来说：我们不能再让这种事发生。我们必须诚实审视自己是怎么输的，这代表什么、意味着什么，以及下次要怎么做。我们会在那些没用的东西上加倍、三倍下注——这种想法我压根没想到。我没想到那个党已经走得那么远，以至于——

cues.en: it couldn't actually, you know, if you imagine that he's orange Hitler, you would think orange Hitler would be the occasion to think deeply and question hypotheses. And I really have been shocked at the extent to which that didn't happen. So maybe I got my own party wrong on that front. I didn't know that we were this far gone, but yeah, no, I mean, it's, it's, I think there's still a lot of time to do that. Um, and I, I keep thinking that, uh, you know, we are at some point where, where the distractions
cues.zh: 它实际上没法——你知道，如果你把他想象成橙色 Hitler，你会以为橙色 Hitler 应该成为深入思考、质疑假设的契机。而这件事竟然没有发生，我真的很震惊。所以也许在这方面我看错了自己的党。我不知道我们已经走得这么远，不过，对，不，我是说，这……我觉得还有很多时间去做这件事。呃，我还一直在想，呃，你知道，我们已经到了某个时刻，那些分散注意力的东西——

cues.en: aren't going to work as well. I think the big distraction on the left over the last 40, 50 years have been forms of identity politics where we don't look at the country as a whole, we look at parts of it, and it's sort of been a way of, I think, obscuring these questions of stagnation. Fair enough, what's the right? I would say the right wing.
cues.zh: 不会那么管用了。我认为过去四五十年里，左派最大的干扰就是各种身份政治，我们不看整个国家，只看它的部分，我觉得这某种程度上遮蔽了停滞这些问题。说得对，那右派呢？我会说是右翼。

cues.en: distraction technique has been, I would say something like American exceptionalism, which is, you know, this doctrine that the US is this singular exceptional country. It's so, so terrific. So wonderful. It does everything so incredibly well that you shouldn't ask any, any difficult questions, any questions at all. And you know, it's, if you want the it's, it's, I think it in theological or epistemological terms, you can compare it to
cues.zh: 转移注意力的一种手段，我想可以说是所谓的“美国例外论”，也就是认为美国是一个独一无二、极其例外的国家。它太棒了，太美好了，把所有事情都做得无可挑剔，以至于你根本不该问任何尖锐的问题，甚至不该有任何疑问。如果你想从神学或认识论的角度来看，我认为你可以把它比作

cues.en: the radical monotheism of the God of the Old Testament, where it means that God is so radically unique that you can't know anything about him. You can't talk about God's attributes. You can't say anything about him whatsoever. And if the United States is radically exceptional, then in a similar way, you can say nothing about it whatsoever. And there may be all these things on the ground that seem crazy where we have people who are exceptionally overweight. We have
cues.zh: 旧约圣经中上帝那种绝对的一神论，意思是上帝是如此绝对独一无二，以至于你无法对他有任何认知。你不能去谈论上帝的属性，关于他你什么都不能说。如果美国是绝对例外的，那么同理，关于它你也什么都不能妄加评判。即便现实中存在着各种看似疯狂的现象：比如我们有着异乎寻常的肥胖人群，我们有着

cues.en: We have subway systems that are exceptionally expensive to build. We have universities that are exceptionally sociopathic. I mean, you don't have the student debt problem in any other country. You know, we have a trade regime that's exceptionally bad for our country. Like, no other country has self-destructive this. There are all these things that we somehow don't ask. So I think exceptionalism somehow led to this country that was exceptionally unselfaware.
cues.zh: 造价极其昂贵的地铁系统，我们有着极其冷血反社会的高校体制——我是说，其他任何国家都不会有如此严重的助学贷款问题。我们的贸易体制也极其不利于本国利益，没有任何一个国家会像这样自我毁灭。面对这一切，我们却不知为何视而不见、从不发问。因此我认为，例外论在某种程度上导致了这个国家陷入了极度的缺乏自知。

cues.en: And that's, and so, you know, there's, you know, greatness is adjacent to exceptionalism, but it's actually still quite different because many countries can be great. And great is more, it's more of a scale and there's some, something you measure it against. Whereas exceptional, it's just completely incommensurate with anything else. And, and, and I think that's, that's gotten us into a very, very bad cul de sac.
cues.zh: 所以你看，“伟大”虽然和“例外”相近，但实际上截然不同，因为很多国家都可以是伟大的。“伟大”更多是一个相对的刻度，是有衡量标准的；而“例外”则是完全不可比拟、无法衡量的。我认为，正是这种思想把我们带进了一条非常糟糕的死胡同。

cues.en: I think that there's a way in which that sort of exceptionalism has ended on the right. And we've moved beyond that. And I'm hopeful that in a similar way, the left will move beyond identity politics, even though right now it feels like the monster is flopping about more violently than ever. Even though I think it might be its death throes, but maybe not. Yeah. It could be that it's gotten very strong or it could be on its last legs and it might as well go for broke. Yes.
cues.zh: 我觉得这种例外论在右翼阵营中已经在某种程度上走向了终结，我们已经走出了那个阶段。我也同样希望，左翼有朝一日能够超越身份政治，尽管眼下感觉这头怪兽还在前所未有地疯狂挣扎。虽然我觉得这可能是它的回光返照，但也说不准。是的，它可能变得极其强大，也可能已是强弩之末、索性孤注一掷。没错。

cues.en: Let me return back to the line of inquiry. Sorry, I'm just enjoying so much hearing what you have to say. Some of it's new to me. The theories that might be portals into a different way of looking at the world. One of them that you brought into my, I've never heard of before, was Gerard's various theories.
cues.zh: 言归正传，抱歉，听你讲这些实在太有意思了，有些观点对我来说也是全新的。那些可能成为看待世界全新视角的理论，其中一个你让我接触到的、我以前从未听说过的，就是 Girard 的各种理论。

cues.en: And I wonder if you might say you've often credited your success in business to how you understood and you applied Girard. I mean, obviously he didn't have this kind of level of business success. So can you talk a little bit about your personal relationship to René Girard's theories as a portal into a different way of seeing the world? Well, let's say a little bit about the theory. So it was sort of this theory of human psychology as deeply mimetic where you sort of,
cues.zh: 我想问的是，你经常把商业上的成功归功于对吉拉尔理论的理解与应用。我的意思是，他显然没有达到这种商业成就。那么，你能谈谈你与勒内·吉拉尔理论的个人渊源吗？它是如何成为你换个视角看世界的入口的？好吧，我们先简单聊聊这个理论。它大体上是说人类心理具有极强的“模仿性”，也就是你……

cues.en: You copy other people. So just for the folks at home, mimetic as in mime, rather than mimetic as in meme. Yes. Well, they're probably closely related, but you imitate people, but you imitate, that's how you learn to speak as a child. You copy your parents' language. That's how, um, but then you also imitate desire. And then, um, there are sort of all sorts of aspects of mimesis that can lead to sort of mass violence, mass insanity. So it has, it's, it's both what enables human culture to function.
cues.zh: 你会模仿其他人。这里给屏幕前的观众说明一下，“模仿”（mimetic）是来自哑剧（mime），而不是模因（meme）。是的。不过它们可能渊源很深。但你会模仿他人，甚至可以说，孩童正是通过模仿学会说话的。你模仿父母的语言。正是这样……但随后你也会模仿欲望。而且，模仿的各个维度还可能引发群体性暴力、集体性癫狂。所以，它既是人类文化得以维系运转的基石……

cues.en: but it also is quite dangerous. And when I came across this sort of constellation of ideas as an undergraduate at Stanford, my biases were sort of libertarian, classic liberal, only individuals exist, individuals are radically autonomous, can think for themselves. And so this was both, it was sort of a powerful corrective to that intellectually.
cues.zh: 但同时也极具危险性。当我在斯坦福读本科接触到这一整套思想时，我当时的认知偏向于自由意志主义、古典自由主义，认为世上只有个体存在，个体高度自治，能够独立思考。因此，无论从哪个角度看，这在思想层面上都给了我强有力的矫正。

cues.en: But then it also worked on an existential level where you sort of realize, wow, there are all these ways that I've been hyper-mimetic. I've been hyper-tracked. Why am I at Stanford? Why does this matter so much? Why am I doing all the things I'm doing? And it's a prism through which one looks at a lot of things that I found to be quite helpful over recent decades. I think the preference falsification, you can...
cues.zh: 但它同时也在存在主义层面上起到了作用，让你意识到：天呐，我在太多方面都极度随波逐流、深受模仿机制影响了。我一直按部就班地活着。我为什么会在斯坦福？这为什么这么重要？我为什么要做我正在做的所有事情？在过去的几十年里，我发现这是一个审视许多事物的绝佳棱镜。我认为“偏好伪装”同样可以……

cues.en: think of in mimetic terms where, you know, everybody goes along with what everybody else thinks. And then you can get these sort of chaotic points where all of a sudden things can shift much faster than you would think possible because they're all these dynamics that are not, uh, you know, not simply rational. It's not quite correct to, to model people as these sort of classical atoms or something like that. It's more entangled. Do you
cues.zh: 用模仿理论来解释，大家往往人云亦云。接着就会出现那种混沌的临界点，局势突然以超乎想象的速度发生剧变，因为存在着所有这些并非……呃，并非纯粹理性的动态机制。如果把人建模成古典主义式的独立原子之类的东西，那是很不准确的。人与人之间的关系要更加纠缠不清。你……

cues.en: What would be a good way for people listening at home to start to get into Gerard's philosophy if they were interested? Well, there are, you know, there's sort of a number of different books that Gerard wrote. I think the magisterial one is probably things hidden since the foundation of the world. So it's this truth of mimesis and violence and the ways, so it's sort of part psychology, part anthropology, part history.
cues.zh: 对于在屏幕前收听、并且感兴趣的观众来说，要入门吉拉尔的哲学，最好的切入点是什么？嗯，你知道的，吉拉尔写过好几本不同的书。我认为最具代表性的集大成之作大概是《自世界奠基以来的隐秘之事》。它揭示了模仿与暴力的真相以及诸种机制，所以它既有心理学成分，也有人类学和历史学的成分。

cues.en: All portal I should point out because they're all hidden. It's a portal onto the past, onto human origins, and our history. It's a portal onto the present, onto the interpersonal dynamics of psychology. It's a portal onto the future in terms of, are we going to let these mimetic desires run amok and head towards apocalyptic violence?
cues.zh: 我得指出，所有门户都是隐藏的。它是一扇通向过去的门户，通向人类起源和我们的历史；是一扇通向现在的门户，通向心理学中的人际动态；也是一扇通向未来的门户——我们会不会放任这些模仿性欲望失控，走向末日式暴力？

cues.en: even the entire planet can no longer absorb the violence that we can unleash. Or are we going to learn from this and transcend this in a way where we get to some very different place? And so it has a sense that, you know, both danger and hope for the future as well. So it is sort of this panoramic theory on a lot of ways, super powerful and just extraordinarily different from what one would
cues.zh: 甚至整个星球都已无法承受我们能释放出的暴力。还是说，我们会从中学习并超越它，从而抵达一个非常不同的境地？所以它给人一种感觉：既有危险，也有对未来的希望。所以它在很多方面算是一种全景式理论，极其强大，而且和人们通常会以为的截然不同。

cues.en: Normally here there was, you know, there was, there was sort of like almost a cult like element where you had, you know, these people who are followers of Gerard and there was sort of a sense that, you know, we had, we had figured out the truth about the world in a way that nobody else did. And that, you know, that, that was generative and, and, and very powerful. You know, it's always, there's parts of it that are unhealthy, but, but, uh, it was, um, uh,
cues.zh: 通常在这里，你知道，会有一种几乎像邪教一样的元素：有这些 Gerard 的追随者，还有一种感觉——我们以别人都没做到的方式看透了世界的真相。而那……那很有生成力，也非常强大。你知道，它总有……有些部分是不健康的，但是，呃，它当时，嗯……

cues.en: it has sort of an incredible dynamism. And then just you are aware that maybe things are so different from how they appear to be that there may be a portal out there. There may be, you know. Well, it was shocking to me. I mean, the first time I heard about it, you invited me to a conference that you were keeping quiet. And I was in the news and there was quite a lot of...
cues.zh: 它有一种不可思议的活力。然后你意识到，也许事情和表面看起来如此不同，以至于外面可能存在一扇门户。可能会有，你知道。嗯，这对我来说很震撼。我是说，我第一次听说时，你邀请我去参加一个你一直没声张的会议。而我当时上了新闻，外面有很多……

cues.en: anger and furor that I had done something wrong. And you waited a few days to give a talk and you talked about scapegoating and the mechanism by which violence that might be visited upon the many is visited upon the one. And then you also started talking about the king as if he is sort of scapegoating and waiting.
cues.zh: 愤怒和狂怒，认为我做错了事。而你等了几天才做演讲，你讲了替罪羊机制，以及可能落到多数人身上的暴力，是如何落到一个人身上的。然后你还开始谈论国王，好像他有点在充当替罪羊、在等待。

cues.en: so that the king is not necessarily something that one would want to be. And I found it absolutely fascinating because it turned so many ideas on their heads that I got angry at you. Why hadn't you told me this earlier when I'd been through three sleepless nights before I'd heard the theory? So I found it instantly applicable, particularly if you're the sort of person who's likely to get scapegoated by not taking refuge in the herd. Do you think it has more relevance to people who are struggling to...
cues.zh: 所以国王未必是人们会想成为的角色。我觉得这绝对迷人，因为它颠覆了太多观念，以至于我对你生气了。你为什么不早点告诉我？在听到这个理论之前，我已经熬过了三个不眠之夜。所以我发现它立刻就能用，尤其如果你属于那种不躲进人群、就容易被当成替罪羊的人。你觉得它对那些正在努力……的人更有意义吗？

cues.en: Like break out as individuals because of the possibility of being picked off, you know, I I think um Well, I think it has universal I think it I think it is universally truly has some sort of universal relevance. I think the problems of violence and scapegoating are are universal problems it is um, It's probably the case. There's certain types of people who are
cues.zh: 比如作为个体突围，因为有可能被挑出来除掉，你知道，我……我觉得，嗯，我觉得它有普遍——我觉得它确实具有某种普遍意义。我认为暴力和替罪羊问题是普遍问题，它是，嗯。情况很可能是这样：有某些类型的人……

cues.en: more likely to become scapegoats, but it's not an absolute thing. And so there's always, you could say there's an arbitrariness about scapegoating because the scapegoat is supposed to represent, to stand in for everybody. And so the scapegoat has to be perceived as someone who's radically other, but then also has to somehow emerge from within the group. And so there are times when the scapegoat
cues.zh: 更容易成为替罪羊，但这不是绝对的。所以总是——你可以说，替罪羊机制带有任意性，因为替罪羊本应代表、代替所有人。因此，替罪羊必须被看作某种彻底的他者，但同时又必须以某种方式来自群体内部。所以有时候，替罪羊……

cues.en: is this sort of outlier, extreme insider, extreme outsider, king slash criminal or whatever personality. And that's probably a dangerous sort of thing. It's like Abraham Lincoln, the incredible orator who's also grows up in a log cabin. So these sort of extreme contrasts are often people who are at risk of this maybe more than others.
cues.zh: 就是这种异类、极端的内部人、极端的外部人、国王/罪犯或无论什么人格。而这大概是种危险的东西。就像 Abraham Lincoln，了不起的演说家，同时又在原木小屋里长大。所以这类极端反差的人，往往比其他人更容易面临这种风险。

cues.en: And then at the same time, you know, because these are sort of mob like dynamics, there is sort of a way in which, you know, it's not like anyone's really safe from the violence. Right. Ever. No, no one's completely safe. I think that's quite quite true. But yes, it's it's it's it's it's yes. But there is a thought that one of the sort of history ideas that Gerard had that is that
cues.zh: 而且与此同时，你知道，因为这有点像乌合之众的动态，在某种程度上，没有人能真正免于这种暴力，对吧？永远都不行。没错，没人是绝对安全的，我认为非常准确。不过，是的，确实如此，但吉拉尔提出的一个历史观点是：

cues.en: is that there's a dynamic to this process where scapegoating, it only works when people don't understand it. And so there's sort of, as you understand it better, it works less well, or it has to get displaced into other dimensions. And so, if you have a witch hunt, say, we need to find a witch to bring back peace to the community, that's sort of a psychosocial understanding of what you're doing.
cues.zh: 在这个过程中存在一种动态机制，即替罪羊机制只有在人们不理解它时才起作用；因此，随着你越发理解它，它的效果就越差，或者必须转移到其他维度去；所以，如果你搞猎巫行动，声称“我们需要找个女巫来恢复社区的和平”，这种做法算是一种社会心理学层面的自我认知，

cues.en: is actually counterproductive with the witch hunt itself. The witch hunt is supposed to be a theological epiphany that God's telling you who the witch is. If you think of it as some sort of psychosocial control mechanism, then it won't work anymore. And so a metaphor that Gerard uses is that the sacred is like phlogiston and violence is like oxygen. But it only...
cues.zh: 但这实际上与猎巫行动本身背道而驰；猎巫原本应该是一种神学上的神启，是上帝在告诉你谁是女巫；如果你把它看作某种社会心理控制机制，它就失效了；所以吉拉尔用过一个隐喻，他说神圣就像“燃素”，而暴力就像“氧气”，但它唯独……

cues.en: works in a world where it's misunderstood. And so if you understand scapegoating, you end up in a world where it works less and less well. And the kind of political and cultural institutions that are that are linked to it will will tend to unravel. You know, I think one of the one of the sort of ways in which this this has happened a great deal in, you know, in modernity.
cues.zh: 唯独在一个人们产生误解的世界里才奏效；因此，一旦你理解了替罪羊机制，你所处的世界中这套机制就会越来越不灵光，而与之挂钩的政治和文化体制往往就会逐渐瓦解；我认为在现代社会中，这种情况大量发生的方式之一……

cues.en: is that we scapegoat the scapegoaters, sort of go up one level of abstraction. And that sort of always makes it a little bit more complicated. And so if we go after the people who were the historical oppressors, the historical victimizers, that's often a super powerful way. And it's like slightly too complicated. There was a Bill Clinton formulation of this. We must unite against those who seek to divide us.
cues.zh: 就是我们去把“制造替罪羊的人”当成替罪羊，相当于上升了一个抽象层次，这往往会让事情变得更复杂一些；所以如果我们去清算那些历史上的压迫者、历史上的施害者，这通常会是一种极具威力的方式，而且稍微有点过于复杂了；比尔·克林顿曾对此有过一句表述：“我们必须团结起来，对抗那些试图分裂我们的人”；

cues.en: which is on some level self-contradictory, but then it's just a little bit too hard for people to fully disentangle. And that's sort of one way that I think it still sort of works, even though, you know, it's again, when everyone sees these moves, when everyone understands them, it just doesn't work that well anymore. So it's like saying, would you like me to prescribe you a placebo?
cues.zh: 这在某种程度上是自相矛盾的，但对大众来说又稍微有点难以彻底理清；我认为这也是它依然能起效的一种方式，尽管同样地，当所有人都看穿这些招数、所有人都心知肚明时，它就不怎么管用了；这就像在说：“你想让我给你开点安慰剂吗？”

cues.en: In other words, that probably does not work very well. That doesn't work very well. That probably does not work very well. And, uh, but then the other part of it that I find terrifying, which is, but also interesting is that implicit in this framework is that there is a minimal level of violence needed to accomplish an end and that the scapegoating mechanism, while entirely unjust has the virtue of being minimal in this, that the horror is visited upon the individual. Yes. Yes.
